intro: Every skater solves physics problems with their body. Standing on a narrow board, a rider keeps their center of mass over four small wheels. Leaning into a carve, they let the trucks steer and let friction pull them around a curve. Popping a 180, they twist against the ground and then ride the spin they carry into the air. Pumping a bowl, they gain speed without ever putting a foot down.

This unit names the ideas behind those moves: center of mass and base of support, the geometry of trucks, centripetal force, the limits of grip, speed wobble, torque, angular momentum and moment of inertia. You will work through real numbers in meters, seconds, kilograms and newtons, using g = 9.8 m/s². You will also learn how to set up trucks, calm a wobble, pump a bowl and practice a frontside 180 step by step, with safety first.

By the end you will be able to explain why a board turns when you lean, calculate the inward force a carve needs, predict how much faster a skater spins when they tuck, and show where the energy of a pump comes from.
bigQuestion: How do balance, turning and spinning on a skateboard follow the same laws of motion that govern every moving object?

words.d: the point where an object's weight acts as if it were all gathered in one place
the area on the ground outlined by everything touching it, such as feet or wheels
the large bolt that holds a truck together and passes through the bushings and hanger
rubbery rings around the kingpin that let the hanger tilt and then push it back to center
the inward force that keeps an object moving in a curve, pointing toward the center
a number, written μ, that describes how strongly two surfaces grip
a fast side-to-side shaking of the board that tends to grow at higher speeds
the twisting effect of a force; force times lever arm
the amount of spin an object carries; moment of inertia times angular velocity
how hard it is to change an object's spin; larger when mass is spread far from the axis

test.q: A skater tips over when the line down from the center of mass:
choices: Falls outside the base of support
test.why: Gravity tips an object once its center of mass is no longer above its base of support.

test.q: What makes a skateboard turn when the rider leans?
choices: The wheels get bigger on one side
The hangers swing on a slanted line and twist the axles
The bearings stop on one side
test.why: Truck geometry turns a tilt of the deck into a twist of the axles, which steers the board.

test.q: Turning the kingpin nut counterclockwise makes the trucks:
choices: Looser, so the board turns more easily
Tighter, so the board turns less
test.why: Loosening the nut lets the bushings relax, so a smaller lean turns the board.

test.q: A 70 kg rider carves at 3 m/s on a 3 m radius. What inward force is needed?
What supplies the centripetal force on a carving skateboard?
choices: Friction between the wheels and the ground
test.why: The ground grips the wheels and pushes them toward the center of the turn.

test.q: If the coefficient of friction were about 0.5, what is the largest turning acceleration on level ground?
test.why: The grip limit is μg = 0.5 × 9.8 = 4.9 m/s².

test.q: During speed wobble, a helpful move is to:
choices: Shift your weight onto the tail
Crouch low and press gently on the front foot
test.why: A low stance with gentle front-foot pressure calms the wobble; sharp corrections and back-foot weight feed it.

choices: The twisting effect of a force, force times lever arm
test.why: Torque equals force times the lever arm and is what changes a spin.

test.q: Why can't a skater start spinning once they are in the air?
choices: There is no outside torque to add angular momentum
Their moment of inertia is zero
test.why: With no ground to push on, nothing outside can twist the skater, so angular momentum stays fixed.

test.q: A spinning skater's moment of inertia drops from 4.0 to 2.0 kg·m². The spin rate:
test.why: L = Iω stays fixed, so halving I doubles ω.

test.q: What is the moment of inertia of a 4 kg weight held 0.5 m from the axis?
Where does the extra energy of a faster spin come from when a skater tucks?
choices: Work done by the skater's muscles pulling in
test.why: Pulling the arms and legs inward takes work, and that work becomes spin energy.

test.q: Why does standing tall in the curve of a bowl add speed?
choices: The legs push against a larger force there than they give back when crouching
It lowers the coefficient of friction
It adds torque from the air
test.why: The deck pushes harder in the curve, so standing there does more work than crouching later returns; the extra becomes kinetic energy.

test.q: A regular rider rolls toward a curb with the curb on the heel side. The rider is riding:
test.why: Backside means the back and heels face the obstacle.

test.q: In a frontside 180 ollie, what is the order of the turn?
test.why: The shoulders lead, the hips follow, and the board follows the hips.

write.prompt: Pick one move from this unit: a carve, a frontside 180 ollie, or pumping a bowl. Explain how to do it step by step, using front foot and back foot, and then explain the physics behind it with one worked example that shows every step of the arithmetic.
tips: Start with the safety gear and the place you would practice.
Write the steps in order with First, Next, Then and Finally.
Name the physics idea: centripetal force, angular momentum or work and energy.
Show each number with its unit, such as m/s, kg or N.
End by explaining what a common mistake does to the physics.
